text: A single rotation of Venus takes about 243 Earth days, which is longer than its year of about 225 Earth days.
Sunlight takes about 8 minutes and 20 seconds to travel from the Sun to Earth.
Neutron stars are so dense that a teaspoon of their material would weigh billions of tonnes on Earth.
Olympus Mons on Mars rises about 22 km, roughly two and a half times the height of Mount Everest above sea level.
Saturn's average density is lower than that of water.
The Moon is drifting away from Earth by about 3.8 cm per year, measured by bouncing lasers off reflectors left by Apollo astronauts.
Jupiter's Great Red Spot is a storm wider than Earth that has been observed continuously for more than 150 years.
The Sun contains about 99.8% of all the mass in our solar system.
Light from the Andromeda Galaxy reaching your eyes tonight left it about 2.5 million years ago.
Uranus spins on its side, with its rotational axis tilted about 98 degrees.
A year on Mercury lasts only about 88 Earth days.
The International Space Station circles Earth about every 90 minutes, so its crew can see around 16 sunrises a day.
Valles Marineris on Mars is a canyon system about 4,000 km long, roughly the width of the continental United States.
Mars's moon Phobos is slowly spiraling inward and is expected to break apart or crash into Mars in roughly 50 million years.
Venus is the hottest planet, at about 465 degrees Celsius, even though Mercury is closer to the Sun. Its thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat.
Voyager 1, launched in 1977, is the most distant human-made object, now more than 24 billion km from Earth.
The observable universe is estimated to be about 93 billion light-years across.
The universe is about 13.8 billion years old, based on measurements of the cosmic microwave background.
The Moon always shows the same face to Earth because it is tidally locked: it rotates once for every orbit.
Mercury and Venus are the only planets in our solar system with no moons.
Jupiter has the shortest day of any planet, rotating once in just under 10 hours.
Neptune has the fastest winds measured in the solar system, reaching more than 2,000 km per hour.
Saturn's rings are mostly water ice and span hundreds of thousands of kilometers, yet in most places they are only about 10 meters to 1 km thick.
Titan, Saturn's largest moon, has lakes and seas of liquid methane and ethane on its surface.
Jupiter's moon Europa likely hides a salty ocean beneath its icy shell that may hold more water than all of Earth's oceans.
Halley's Comet returns roughly every 76 years. Its next appearance in the inner solar system is expected in 2061.
The Milky Way is estimated to contain somewhere between 100 and 400 billion stars.
At the center of the Milky Way sits Sagittarius A*, a black hole about 4 million times the mass of the Sun.
Sunsets on Mars look bluish, because fine dust in its atmosphere scatters blue light toward the direction of the Sun.
Stars twinkle because of turbulence in Earth's atmosphere. Planets twinkle less because they appear as tiny disks rather than points.
The temperature at the Sun's core is about 15 million degrees Celsius.
Pluto takes about 248 Earth years to complete one orbit around the Sun.
Pluto has a vast heart-shaped region of bright ice, first seen clearly by NASA's New Horizons spacecraft in 2015.
Ganymede, Jupiter's largest moon, is bigger than the planet Mercury.
The first image of a black hole, released in 2019, showed the one at the center of galaxy M87, about 55 million light-years away.
Astronauts can temporarily grow a few centimeters taller in orbit as their spines decompress without gravity.
Earth is closest to the Sun in early January, during winter in the Northern Hemisphere.
Seasons are caused by Earth's axial tilt of about 23.4 degrees, not by changes in our distance from the Sun.
Octopuses have three hearts and blue blood, which uses a copper-based molecule called hemocyanin to carry oxygen.
Tardigrades can survive near-complete dehydration by curling into a dormant state called a tun, then revive when water returns.
Recent estimates suggest the human body holds roughly as many bacterial cells as human cells, overturning the old claim of ten to one.
Honeybees share the direction and distance of food sources with a movement called the waggle dance.
Sea otters sometimes hold paws or wrap themselves in kelp while resting so they do not drift apart.
Humans and chimpanzees share about 98 to 99 percent of their DNA sequences.
Crows can recognize individual human faces and remember people who treated them poorly for years.
Blue whales are the largest animals known to have ever lived, reaching about 30 meters long.
A blue whale's heart can weigh around 180 kg, making it one of the largest hearts in the animal kingdom.
The jellyfish Turritopsis dohrnii can revert from its adult form to an earlier polyp stage, potentially more than once.
Most plants partner with mycorrhizal fungi, which help roots absorb water and nutrients in exchange for sugars.
The cells lining your stomach and intestines are replaced every few days.
Babies are born with around 270 to 300 bones and cartilage pieces, many of which fuse into the 206 bones of an adult.
The human brain is about 2% of body weight but uses roughly 20% of the body's energy.
Axolotls can regenerate entire limbs, parts of their spinal cord, and even sections of their heart.
Hummingbirds are among the very few birds that can hover in place and fly backward.
Koala fingerprints are so similar to human fingerprints that they can be hard to tell apart, even under a microscope.
A mantis shrimp's strike is so fast that it creates collapsing cavitation bubbles in the water, adding a second impact.
Elephants communicate with low-frequency rumbles that can travel several kilometers.
Pando, a grove of quaking aspen in Utah, is a single organism: tens of thousands of trunks sharing one root system.
Flamingos get their pink color from carotenoid pigments in the algae and crustaceans they eat.
Cats cannot taste sweetness because the gene for one of their sweet taste receptors does not work.
Dolphins can sleep with one half of their brain at a time, letting them keep surfacing to breathe.
Wood frogs can survive having much of their body water freeze in winter. Their hearts stop, then restart when they thaw.
Greenland sharks may be the longest-lived vertebrates, with estimated lifespans of several centuries.
Some Great Basin bristlecone pines in California are more than 4,800 years old.
Slime molds, which have no brain, can find efficient routes through mazes to reach food.
Platypuses hunt with their eyes closed, using electroreceptors in their bills to sense the tiny electric fields of prey.
In seahorses, the male carries the developing young in a pouch and gives birth to them.
If you uncoiled the DNA in a single human cell, it would stretch about 2 meters.
Mammalian red blood cells have no nucleus, and each one lives about 120 days.
Butterflies taste with sensors on their feet, which helps them choose where to lay eggs.
Leafcutter ants do not eat the leaves they cut. They use them to grow a fungus garden, which they eat.
Owls cannot move their eyes within their sockets, so they rotate their heads up to about 270 degrees instead.
Bats are the only mammals capable of true, sustained flight.
Sea stars have no blood. They move nutrients using a water vascular system filled mostly with seawater.
Giraffes have the same number of neck vertebrae as humans: seven. Each one is just much longer.
A teaspoon of healthy soil can contain more microorganisms than there are people on Earth.
Light travels about 300,000 km per second in a vacuum, fast enough to circle Earth about 7.5 times in one second.
Clocks on GPS satellites run faster than clocks on the ground by about 38 microseconds a day, and the system must correct for it.
Old windows are sometimes thicker at the bottom because of how the glass was made, not because glass slowly flows.
A lightning bolt can heat the surrounding air to about 30,000 degrees Celsius, around five times hotter than the Sun's surface.
Thunder is the sound of air expanding explosively after being superheated by lightning.
Sound travels about 1 km in 3 seconds, so you can estimate a storm's distance by counting between lightning and thunder.
Rainbows are actually full circles. The ground usually hides the lower half, but pilots can sometimes see the whole ring.
The sky looks blue because air molecules scatter shorter blue wavelengths of sunlight far more than longer red ones.
Absolute zero is minus 273.15 degrees Celsius. Physics says it can be approached but never reached exactly.
On the Moon in 1971, astronaut David Scott dropped a hammer and a feather together, and they hit the ground at the same time.
Atoms are mostly empty space. If a nucleus were the size of a marble, the whole atom would be roughly the size of a stadium.
Sound travels about 343 meters per second in air but more than four times faster in water.
Quantum tunneling, where particles slip through energy barriers, is essential to the nuclear fusion that powers the Sun.
Water expands by about 9% when it freezes, which is why ice floats and frozen pipes can burst.
Trillions of neutrinos, mostly from the Sun, pass harmlessly through your body every second.
Superconductors carry electric current with zero resistance when cooled below a critical temperature.
Helium cooled to a superfluid state flows without friction and can creep up and over the walls of its container.
Polarized sunglasses cut glare because light reflecting off flat surfaces like water is largely polarized horizontally.
A metal spoon feels colder than a wooden one at the same temperature because metal draws heat from your skin faster.
A sonic boom is not a one-time event. A supersonic aircraft drags a continuous boom along the ground behind it.
A mirror does not really swap left and right. It reverses front and back along the direction you face it.
The Doppler effect explains why a passing siren's pitch drops: sound waves bunch up ahead of it and stretch out behind.
The Sun converts about 4 million tonnes of mass into energy every second through nuclear fusion.
Energy made in the Sun's core can take tens of thousands of years or more to reach the surface, then about 8 minutes to reach us.
The old claim that bumblebees should not be able to fly came from oversimplified math. Their wings create lift with swirling vortices.
Light travels through diamond at only about 41% of its speed in a vacuum, which helps give diamonds their sparkle.
Scientists have cooled atoms in laboratories to billionths of a degree above absolute zero, colder than anywhere known in nature.
Gravity on the Moon is about one-sixth as strong as on Earth.
You weigh slightly less at the equator than at the poles, thanks to Earth's rotation and its bulge at the middle.
Electrons in a household wire drift at only a fraction of a millimeter per second, even though the electrical signal travels extremely fast.
Most of a proton's mass comes from the energy of the quarks and gluons inside it, not from the rest mass of the quarks themselves.
Microwave ovens heat food mainly by making water molecules rapidly rotate back and forth, which produces heat.
The swirling colors on a soap bubble come from light waves reflecting off its inner and outer surfaces and interfering.
Ice is slippery largely because of a thin, liquid-like layer on its surface. Pressure from skates alone cannot explain it.
For small swings, a pendulum's period depends on its length, not on how heavy it is.
Light carries momentum. In 2010, Japan's IKAROS spacecraft used a solar sail pushed by sunlight to travel through space.
Helium was first detected in the Sun's spectrum in 1868, decades before it was found on Earth.
Gold is so malleable that a single gram can be hammered into a sheet roughly one square meter in size.
Diamond and graphite are both pure carbon. The only difference is how their atoms are arranged.
Water is one of very few substances whose solid form is less dense than its liquid form.
Honey can keep for a very long time because its low water content and acidity make it hard for microbes to grow.
Liquid oxygen is pale blue and is attracted to strong magnets.
Gallium is a metal that melts at about 30 degrees Celsius, so a piece of it can melt in your hand.
Mercury and bromine are the only elements that are liquid at standard room temperature and pressure.
Bananas are very slightly radioactive because they contain potassium, a small fraction of which is radioactive potassium-40.
Fluorine is the most electronegative element and is reactive enough to form compounds with the noble gas xenon.
Part of the earthy smell after rain comes from geosmin, made by soil microbes. Human noses can detect it at extremely low levels.
Cutting onions releases a sulfur compound, syn-propanethial-S-oxide, that irritates your eyes and makes them water.
Hydrogen is the most abundant element in the universe, making up about three-quarters of ordinary matter by mass.
Oxygen is the most abundant element in Earth's crust, accounting for about 46% of its mass.
Stainless steel resists rust because its chromium forms a thin, invisible oxide layer that repairs itself when scratched.
The Statue of Liberty is green because its copper skin reacted with air and moisture to form a protective patina.
Most everyday glass is made mainly from silica, the main ingredient in sand.
Some aerogels are more than 99% air by volume, making them among the lightest solid materials ever made.
Dry ice is solid carbon dioxide. At normal air pressure it skips the liquid phase and turns straight into gas.
Dmitri Mendeleev left gaps in his periodic table and correctly predicted the properties of elements not yet discovered, such as gallium.
Tungsten has the highest melting point of any metal, about 3,422 degrees Celsius.
Water makes up roughly 50 to 60 percent of an adult human's body weight.
By mass, the most common element in the human body is oxygen, at about 65%, mostly because of all the water we contain.
Chili peppers feel hot because capsaicin activates TRPV1, the same receptor that senses painful heat.
Mint feels cool because menthol activates TRPM8, a receptor in your skin and mouth that normally senses cold.
Baking soda and vinegar fizz because the acid reacts with sodium bicarbonate to release carbon dioxide gas.
Firework colors come from metal salts: strontium for red, barium for green, copper for blue, and sodium for yellow.
Pure neon glows red-orange. Many other colors in neon signs come from different gases or from coatings inside the tubes.
Pure water is a poor conductor of electricity. Tap water conducts because of the dissolved minerals in it.
Rust takes up more volume than the iron it forms from, which is why rusting can crack concrete around steel bars.
Ozone is a form of oxygen with three atoms per molecule. The ozone layer absorbs most of the Sun's harmful UV-B radiation.
Teflon was discovered by accident in 1938, when chemist Roy Plunkett found a slippery white solid in a gas cylinder.
Nitrogen makes up about 78% of Earth's atmosphere, while oxygen makes up about 21%.
Fertilizer made with the Haber-Bosch process is estimated to help feed about half of the world's population.
Four chemical elements are named after the small Swedish village of Ytterby: yttrium, ytterbium, terbium, and erbium.
Caffeine keeps you alert mainly by blocking adenosine receptors in the brain, which normally signal tiredness.
Salt melts ice on roads because dissolved salt lowers the temperature at which water freezes.
Water boils at a lower temperature at high altitude. On the summit of Everest, it boils at about 70 degrees Celsius.
Cut apples turn brown because an enzyme called polyphenol oxidase reacts with oxygen in the air.
Earth's magnetic field has flipped many times. The last full reversal happened about 780,000 years ago.
The Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench is nearly 11 km deep, deeper than Mount Everest is tall.
Measured from its base on the ocean floor, Mauna Kea in Hawaii is about 10,000 meters tall, taller than Everest.
Because Earth bulges at the equator, the summit of Chimborazo in Ecuador is the point on land farthest from Earth's center.
Antarctica is the largest desert on Earth, because deserts are defined by low precipitation, not heat.
About 71% of Earth's surface is covered by water.
Only about a quarter of the ocean floor has been mapped in high resolution.
Roughly half of the oxygen we breathe comes from the ocean, mostly produced by tiny phytoplankton.
Earth's rotation is gradually slowing, and the day grows longer by roughly 2 milliseconds per century.
Earth is not a perfect sphere. Its diameter at the equator is about 43 km larger than from pole to pole.
Earth's inner core is about as hot as the surface of the Sun, yet it stays solid because of immense pressure.
Continents drift a few centimeters each year, roughly the rate at which fingernails grow.
The Atlantic Ocean is widening by a few centimeters every year as the plates on either side move apart.
Lake Baikal in Siberia is the world's deepest lake, at about 1,640 meters, and holds around a fifth of Earth's unfrozen surface fresh water.
The Amazon River carries about one-fifth of all the fresh water that rivers deliver to the oceans.
Lightning strikes somewhere on Earth about 40 to 50 times every second.
The Himalayas are still rising by a few millimeters a year as the Indian plate pushes into Asia.
Between about 11,000 and 5,000 years ago, much of the Sahara was green, with grasslands and lakes.
Earth is about 4.54 billion years old.
The oldest known pieces of Earth are tiny zircon crystals from Western Australia, about 4.4 billion years old.
Hawaii's Big Island is still growing as lava from its volcanoes flows into the sea and hardens into new land.
The shore of the Dead Sea lies about 430 meters below sea level, the lowest land elevation on Earth.
The lowest natural air temperature directly measured on Earth was minus 89.2 degrees Celsius, at Vostok Station, Antarctica, in 1983.
Old Faithful in Yellowstone erupts roughly every 60 to 110 minutes, powered by heat from a volcanic hotspot below.
In Iceland, you can walk through rift valleys where the North American and Eurasian plates are pulling apart.
The longest mountain range on Earth is the mid-ocean ridge, about 65,000 km long and almost entirely underwater.
Angel Falls in Venezuela is the world's tallest uninterrupted waterfall on land, with a drop of about 979 meters.
The largest known waterfall is underwater: the Denmark Strait cataract, where cold dense water plunges about 3.5 km.
About half the mass of Earth's atmosphere lies below an altitude of about 5.5 km.
The Antarctic ice sheet holds about 90% of the ice on Earth's surface and roughly 60 to 70 percent of its fresh water.
A mature hurricane can release heat energy at a rate estimated at around 200 times the world's electricity generating capacity.
Snowflakes are six-sided because of the hexagonal way water molecules bond together as they freeze.
A typical fluffy cumulus cloud can hold around 500 tonnes of water, spread out as tiny droplets.
Our relatively large Moon helps stabilize the tilt of Earth's axis, which keeps our climate steadier over long periods.
The supercontinent Pangaea began breaking apart about 200 million years ago.
The 1815 eruption of Mount Tambora in Indonesia cooled the globe and led to 1816 being called the Year Without a Summer.
The strongest earthquake ever recorded struck Chile in 1960, with a magnitude of about 9.5.
The 1883 eruption of Krakatoa was heard nearly 4,800 km away, among the loudest sounds in recorded history.
Earth's north magnetic pole wanders. In recent decades it has drifted toward Siberia by tens of kilometers per year.
In 1947, engineers found a real moth stuck in a Harvard Mark II relay and taped it into the logbook, though the term 'bug' was already in use.
The first website, created by Tim Berners-Lee at CERN, went online in 1991 and has been restored so you can still visit it.
The Apollo Guidance Computer had about 4 KB of erasable memory and 72 KB of read-only memory.
The QWERTY keyboard layout dates back to typewriters developed in the 1870s.
IBM's 3380, introduced in 1980, was among the first hard drives to store over a gigabyte and was about the size of a refrigerator.
Ada Lovelace published what is often considered the first computer program in 1843, for Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine.
The first SMS text message was sent in December 1992. It read: Merry Christmas.
Ray Tomlinson sent the first networked email in 1971 and chose the @ symbol to separate user names from computer names.
A GPS receiver needs signals from at least four satellites to work out its position and the exact time.
Grace Hopper developed one of the first compilers and helped shape COBOL, a language still running in many banks today.
Moore's law observed that transistor counts on chips double about every two years. Modern chips hold tens of billions of transistors.
ENIAC, one of the first general-purpose electronic computers, weighed about 27 tonnes and filled a large room.
The oldest surviving camera photograph, made by Nicephore Niepce in the 1820s, required an exposure of many hours or even days.
The Hubble Space Telescope launched in 1990 with a flawed mirror. Astronauts installed corrective optics in 1993.
The vast majority of intercontinental internet traffic travels through fiber-optic cables laid on the ocean floor, not satellites.
CAPTCHA stands for Completely Automated Public Turing test to tell Computers and Humans Apart.
The first commercial handheld mobile phone, the Motorola DynaTAC 8000X from 1983, weighed nearly 800 grams.
Bluetooth is named after Harald Bluetooth, a Danish king, and its logo combines his runic initials.
Many computer systems count time from January 1, 1970. Systems that store it in 32-bit signed numbers will overflow in 2038.
Velcro was inspired by burrs that stuck to George de Mestral's dog during a walk in the 1940s.
The microwave oven was invented after engineer Percy Spencer noticed a candy bar melting near an active radar magnetron.
The word robot comes from Karel Capek's 1920 play R.U.R. and the Czech word robota, meaning forced labor.
Each Voyager spacecraft carries a Golden Record with sounds, music, and images meant to represent life on Earth.
Linus Torvalds started the Linux kernel in 1991 as a personal hobby project. It now runs most of the world's servers.
One of the first webcams was set up at Cambridge University in 1991 to watch a coffee pot, so people knew when it was full.
The transistor, the building block of modern electronics, was invented at Bell Labs in 1947.
The Jacquard loom of 1804 used punched cards to control weaving patterns, an idea that later inspired early computers.
The first registered .com domain name was symbolics.com, in 1985.
The first product scanned with a UPC barcode at a store checkout, in 1974, was a pack of Wrigley's chewing gum.
Post-it Notes grew out of a weak, reusable adhesive that 3M chemist Spencer Silver created while trying to make a strong one.
The inventors of efficient blue LEDs, which made bright white LED lighting possible, won the 2014 Nobel Prize in Physics.
QR codes were invented in 1994 by Denso Wave to track car parts during manufacturing.
The first message sent over ARPANET in 1969 was LO. The system crashed before the operator could finish typing LOGIN.
The developers of the lithium-ion battery received the 2019 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
The Antikythera mechanism, built in ancient Greece over 2,000 years ago, used gears to predict eclipses and planetary positions.
The first computer mouse, built by Douglas Engelbart's team in the 1960s, had a wooden shell.
Junk email is called spam because of a Monty Python sketch in which the word is repeated over and over.
The International Space Station is often called the most expensive single object ever built, with estimated costs well over 100 billion US dollars.
A modern smartphone has millions of times more memory than the computers that guided the Apollo missions to the Moon.
